text: Nishapur announced itself the way a name announces a man he has never met - familiar in shape, entirely strange in substance. His father had carried this city's name his whole life without ever once, that Farrukh knew of, setting foot inside its walls; and now the son who bore it too was arriving for both of them, nineteen years and one grave too late for it to mean what it might have. The turquoise market alone told him he'd reached somewhere the empire still thought worth keeping - stalls of blue-green stone laid out like a wealth that hadn't yet heard the frontier behind it was failing.

He had expected, walking in, something closer to homecoming. What he felt instead was closer to visiting a stranger's house that happened to share his family's name on the deed - every street a place his father had chosen never to return to, for reasons Farrukh now understood he would never fully recover, no matter how much of this road he retraced.

He thought, without meaning to, of Merv's emptied quarter: a third of a city the present had simply walked past, which he had been given a morning to walk himself and had spent otherwise. He had not expected it to matter. Standing in a street his father had chosen never to come back to, it occurred to him that he had passed up the one place on this road that might have shown him what being walked past actually looked like from the inside.

text: Nishapur ran on two economies at once, and neither one seemed aware of the other. The turquoise trade filled half the bazaar with a wealth that had outlasted every dynasty that ever taxed it; the other half filled with men arguing points of hadith outside the mosque with the same heat other cities reserved for arguing prices. Farrukh understood, watching both at once, that a city could hold its ground against the frontier's failure a while longer than a fortress could - not because it was stronger, but because it had more than one thing worth defending.

He understood the argument here well enough without having watched it made in mud. He would have liked, standing in it now, to have seen it being made.

text: Nishapur's bazaar kept a courier trade as old as the turquoise itself - men who carried nothing but folded paper and other men's trust between cities that never saw each other's coin change hands. Farrukh thought, watching one such courier haggle over a fee to Marw, of his father's suftaja, and then, less expectedly, of Nasuh - four months unpaid, still minding whatever was left of a dead man's shop, because nobody had told him not to. It would cost something to send even a little of it home. He had, by his own accounting, not very much left to send.

text: Twenty dirham, folded into a letter he wrote three times before he was satisfied with it, went west that same afternoon with a courier he paid extra to remember his name. It was not four months of wages. It was not even half. But it was more than a promise, which was the one thing his father's own ledger had apparently never quite managed to be.

He had asked a sarraf in Bost, once, how he kept his own books, and been told - with more patience than the question deserved - that the point of an entry is not the sum but the fact that somebody wrote it down while it was still true. He had been keeping his that way ever since, without quite noticing when the habit started.

text: He opened the ledger again that evening - a habit two cities old now, whether or not it had earned the name yet - and wrote what there was to write about Nasuh: not the coin itself, sent or withheld, but the plain fact of an old man still owed four months nobody in Ghazni had hurried to settle, carried the whole distance from a shop he'd never see again to a city that had never heard of him. Some entries, he was beginning to understand, existed less to be settled than simply to be kept - a way of making sure a debt didn't vanish just because the man it was owed to was two provinces away and unlikely ever to ask.

He had done it once on the road out of Pushang without thinking of it as anything at all: read a drawn-down cistern and a fire put out too carefully, understood who was ahead of him on that ground and why they were keeping off the track, and drawn the water before the eldest of them had to stand in front of a stranger and ask for it. It cost him a quarter of an hour. What it spared them was the asking, and he was beginning to suspect that the asking was the only part of any of this that had ever really been his to give or to withhold.

text: He found somewhere to sleep that first night more by exhaustion than by planning - a corner of a caravanserai courtyard already crowded with better-organized travelers, his own bedroll unrolled between two strangers' baggage because asking after a proper room, this late, felt like one transaction too many for a day that had already asked enough of him. Nishapur, he was beginning to suspect, was not a city that revealed itself in a single day any more than his father had revealed himself in nineteen years of silence.

The next morning, still without proper lodging to his name, Farrukh heard that a teacher kept a {{khaneqah|khaneqah}} near the western quarter, and that anyone was welcome to listen at dusk. There was, first, a smaller matter to settle, or not.

text: He thought of it only once, and only briefly - a wife and children somewhere in this city or the next, who would go on not knowing whatever it was they didn't know, because a stranger at a gate in Sarakhs had decided he already had enough not-knowing of his own to carry. It had felt, at the time, like the honest answer. It still did, mostly. He let the thought go the way he'd let go of everything else on this road that wasn't strictly his to fix, and went to find out what Nishapur's own business wanted from him instead.

Whatever grew there had grown from a start neither of them picked. It made the phrase not strictly his to fix harder to put down than he would have liked.

text: He found them by the third house he asked at - a wife and two children who took the token from his hand with the particular stillness of people who had spent every season since the muster deepened waiting for exactly this kind of stranger to appear at their door, and dreading it in equal measure. She did not ask if her husband still lived. Farrukh understood, watching her not-ask, that she'd already reasoned past the one thing he could tell her - that Bahram had been alive and whole the morning he left Sarakhs - straight through to the truer uncertainty underneath it, the one no stranger arriving weeks later could settle either way.

He had been paid twelve dirham to bring it. The coin had seemed reasonable at a gate in Sarakhs, a fair rate for a detour and a risk, and it had spent exactly like any other coin since. Standing in this doorway, watching a woman decline to ask the only question that mattered to her, he could not make the arithmetic come out the same way twice.

text: She nodded before he'd finished saying it. A message from Merv had reached this door some days before he had - enough warning that a stranger's knock meant less to her than it would have otherwise. It was not much of a mercy, set against everything else the muster had already cost her. It was, Farrukh understood, still a mercy.

There was, before the khaneqah, one more piece of the road still unfinished. Nishapur's courier quarter ran on the same quiet channels every city on this journey had turned out to run on - amana, reputation, and the specific discretion of men who moved other people's business for a living - and it took less asking than Farrukh expected before someone, unprompted, recognized the name he'd carried since Farah. "Mansur," the man said, testing the word like a coin he wasn't sure was genuine. "That's not really a name. It's a signature. Passed hand to hand longer than either of us has been alive, so no single throat ever has to answer for all of it." Farrukh thought of Mihran, months and provinces behind him now, promising that the name would still be true whenever he found it. It was, he supposed, exactly that true - just not in the shape he'd pictured holding still long enough to belong to one man.

He had been at both ends of that now. It had cost him less, each time, than the not-saying would have.

text: He was willing, for a price Farrukh had grown almost used to paying by now, to say what the name had actually carried this time. Six years back, when Rayy's old ruling house fell and the state crucified whichever da'i - missionaries for a banned cause, funded out of Cairo - it could catch in the same season, what survived of both collapses hadn't simply vanished. It had gone underground, and some of it, evidently, still moved as ordinary paper. This particular thread of it wasn't treason, or soldiers, or gold for an uprising - it was money, and letters, meant for the households of the men the state had already crucified. Widows. Orphans. Whatever a household has left once the state has taken the man and everything he owned besides.

Why his father, specifically, Farrukh finally asked - and got, for once, an answer that felt less like information bought than a debt someone else had also been carrying a long time. His father had known one of the crucified men, the courier said - not well, an old trading acquaintance from years before, a kindness owed from some transaction neither man had probably thought worth remembering at the time. When the man's widow needed a way to move money without her own name attached to it, someone had remembered an honest merchant in Ghazni who owed her husband something, once, and had never had the chance to repay it. Ibn Hasan had said yes. Nobody Farrukh spoke to could tell him whether he'd said yes out of guilt, or grief, or plain decency, or fear of what refusing a network like that might have cost him - only that he had kept saying yes, quietly, for longer than a single kindness usually lasts.

He had been given the whole shape of it in Herat, by someone who had decided he could be trusted with all of it at once, and he had carried that knowledge the length of two more cities without ever being able to do anything with it. Hearing it confirmed by a stranger who had no reason to soften it was not relief. It was only the end of the small hope that he had misunderstood.

text: It was, Farrukh understood, walking back out into Nishapur's ordinary afternoon light, a complete enough answer as such answers went, and short of the one thing he actually wanted. He knew now what his father had carried, and roughly why he had first agreed to carry it. He'd shown the courier his mother's seal too, without much hope of more than Mihran had already told him back in Bost - and got exactly that much and no further: a shrug, and confirmation that whatever private hand had once used it, Nishapur's own channels had never carried word of it. Whoever his father had been writing to, personally, stayed exactly as unnamed as the reason he'd first agreed to. What he would never know was what it had cost the man to keep saying yes, year after year, in a shop in Ghazni that had never once let the debt show on its face. Some accounting simply did not survive the man who kept it.

The khaneqah was smaller than the mosque's arguments outside had led him to expect - a plain room, a teacher old enough to have outlived most of his own scandals, and an audience that had stopped needing to be convinced this was worth their evening some years before Farrukh arrived. Others called him controversial, still, in the tone of people repeating an old argument rather than starting a new one - a man who'd praised a heretic long executed, who let his students sing and dance when devotion was supposed to look more like silence, who'd once been reported to the Sultan himself for exactly those things and had somehow talked his way clear of it. He did not call himself sheikh, or master, or anything at all, as far as Farrukh could tell. Others did that for him.

In a drill-yard at Sarakhs he had stood listening to an old ghulam tell a story about a bought boy who had finished as the governor of an entire province, and had admitted to himself, privately, without saying it aloud to anyone in the yard, that he envied it. He had thought at the time the envy was about the province. Sitting here, listening to a man who would not use the word for himself at all explain that the self was the last veil left to get past, he understood it had been about something smaller and considerably harder to put down: the wish to be someone whose name arrived in a room ahead of him. Nobody, son of Nobody, had spent forty years wanting the exact reverse of that, and had a room full of people who came out in the evening to hear him not say it.

text: He walked back out into a Nishapur evening turning over an old letter-writer's lesson from Ghazni against this dusk's teaching, the two of them refusing, however he arranged them, to sit comfortably in the same hand. Avicenna's floating man, stripped of every sense, every borrowed thing, was still supposed to know, without instruction, that he existed - a self so bedrock it survived total sensory erasure. This teacher, in the same city, on the same evening, was arguing the opposite case: that the self was not bedrock at all, but the very thing a man had to work hardest to be rid of. Farrukh had carried the first idea the entire length of a debt, a mystery, and a road two provinces long. He did not know, standing in the dark outside a stranger's khaneqah, which of the two ideas he'd actually been practicing this whole time.

Somewhere behind him, a father's debt he had chosen to carry, a name from Rayy that had finally told him what it carried and roughly why, though never what it had cost the man carrying it to keep saying yes, a token delivered or never asked for at all - and ahead of him, still, whatever the rest of a life spent knowing or unknowing himself actually looked like. He had to decide, walking on, which of two men he'd rather have been the whole time.

He had to decide, walking on, which of two men he'd rather have been the whole time. He had heard this argument once before, outside a shuttered shop in Ghazni, from an old letter-writer who had meant it kindly, and he had told the man to his face that he would rather have had the body than the argument. It had felt like honesty at the time. Standing here, being asked the same question by nobody at all, he could not decide whether the years between had earned him the right to change his answer, or only the habit of expecting to.

text: He chose, in the end, to believe Avicenna's floating man over the teacher at the khaneqah - that whatever had been stripped from him since his father's grave, a name, a fortune, an easy road, the man doing the choosing had never once stopped being someone in particular, and never would, all the way to whatever debt or reckoning still waited past Nishapur's walls. It was not peace, exactly. It was, he decided, close enough to it to keep walking on.

He chose, in the end, to believe the teacher at the khaneqah over Avicenna's floating man - that the self he'd spent this entire road insisting on, defending, negotiating, and occasionally sacrificing for a stranger's sake, had never been the point of any of it, and that whatever peace existed past Nishapur's walls would have to be found by a man who'd finally stopped needing to be anyone in particular to find it. It was not relief, exactly. It was, he decided, close enough to it to keep walking on.
